title: africa fx ghanaian ugandan currencies stay back foot 2026 09 10
text:
ACCRA, Sept 10 (Reuters) - The currencies of Ghana and Uganda are expected to weaken further against the dollar in the next week to Thursday, while those of Kenya ​and Zambia are seen holding steady, traders said.
Ghana's cedi is expected ‌to extend its gradual slide against the dollar on persistent corporate foreign-currency demand.
LSEG data showed the cedi trading at 11.45 to the dollar on Thursday, compared to 11.36 a week earlier.
"The ​cedi remains under mild pressure as corporate FX demand picks up again, ​with the Bank of Ghana's reduced monthly intermediation through its FX ⁠auctions leaving less supply in the market to absorb these flows," said Ronald ​Mensah, a trader at Stanbic Bank Ghana.
Another trader said the cedi could weaken further ​on rising crude oil prices following the recent escalation in the Iran war.
Uganda's shilling is seen weakening on the back of strong dollar demand from energy importers.
Commercial banks quoted the shilling ​at 3,820/3,830 to the U.S. currency, compared with last Thursday's close of 3,775/3,785.
The ​local unit on Thursday weakened past 3,800 against the dollar, pressured by demand from fuel importers ‌and ⁠commercial banks beefing up their hard-currency positions, a trader said.
"We think this energy-related appetite will continue to manifest based on the events unfolding in the Middle East," he said, adding the shilling was likely to test 3,850 to the dollar soon.
Kenya's ​shilling is forecast to ​be steady against ⁠the dollar.
Commercial banks quoted the shilling at 129.30/50 per dollar, barely changed from last Thursday's close of 129.35/55.
Zambia's kwacha is ​also likely to be little changed, as high copper prices ​offset import-related ⁠dollar demand.
On Thursday the currency of Africa's second-largest copper producer was quoted at 19.56 per dollar, compared with 19.37 a week earlier.
"Continued high copper prices and subdued speculative ⁠activity should ​limit the extent of the depreciation, leaving the ​kwacha more likely to consolidate than to enter a sustained weakening trend," Access Bank said in a ​note.
